title: Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter covers the numerical implementation of M-estimation for linear regression models using Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS). It explains how robust regression problems are converted into a sequence of weighted least squares fits and presents the explicit algorithmic steps using Huber's $\psi$-function and the median absolute deviation (MAD). ## The Motivation for Iterative Fitting Ordinary least squares (OLS) estimates the regression coefficients $\beta$ by minimizing the sum of squared residuals: $$\min_{\beta} \sum_{i=1}^n r_i(\beta)^2, \quad \text{where } r_i(\beta) = y_i - x_i^T \beta$$ Because the penalty grows quadratically with the residual magnitude $r_i$, even a single extreme outlier can draw the fitted line away from the bulk of the data. M-estimation replaces the quadratic loss with a less sensitive, robust objective function $\rho$: $$\min_{\beta} \sum_{i=1}^n \rho\left(\frac{r_i}{\sigma}\right)$$ where $\sigma$ is a scale parameter representing the dispersion of the error distribution. Differentiating this objective with respect to $\beta$ and setting the gradient to zero yields the estimating equations: $$\sum_{i=1}^n \psi\left(\frac{r_i}{\sigma}\right) x_i = 0$$ Here, $\psi(u) = \rho'(u)$ is the influence function. Unlike the linear estimating equations of OLS, this system is generally nonlinear in $\beta$ because the residuals appear inside $\psi$. Consequently, the optimal coefficients cannot be solved via a closed-form matrix inversion. ## Reformulation as Weighted Least Squares To solve the nonlinear estimating equations, we define a weight function: $$w(u) = \frac{\psi(u)}{u}$$ Multiplying and dividing the argument of $\psi$ inside the estimating equation produces: $$\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\psi(r_i / \sigma)}{r_i / \sigma} \cdot \left(\frac{r_i}{\sigma}\right) x_i = 0 \implies \sum_{i=1}^n w\left(\frac{r_i}{\sigma}\right) r_i x_i = 0$$ Defining the weights as $w_i = w(r_i / \sigma)$, the condition simplifies to: $$\sum_{i=1}^n w_i (y_i - x_i^T \beta) x_i = 0$$ This expression is identical to the normal equations of a weighted least squares (WLS) problem with observation weights $w_i$. However, the weights $w_i$ themselves depend on the unknown coefficients $\beta$ through the residuals $r_i$. This circular dependence motivates an iterative scheme: 1. Given current estimates $\hat{\beta}^{(k)}$, compute the residuals $r_i^{(k)} = y_i - x_i^T \hat{\beta}^{(k)}$. 2. Estimate the scale parameter $\hat{\sigma}$ robustly from the residuals. 3. Compute standardized residuals $z_i = r_i^{(k)} / \hat{\sigma}$. 4. Evaluate weights $w_i = \psi(z_i) / z_i$. 5. Update $\hat{\beta}^{(k+1)}$ by solving the weighted linear regression of $y$ on $X$ using weights $w_i$. 6. Repeat until the estimated coefficients stabilize. ## Components of the Algorithm ### Robust Scale Estimation: The MAD The standard deviation cannot be used to estimate $\sigma$ because it is sensitive to the very outliers M-estimation seeks to downweight. Instead, the algorithm uses the Median Absolute Deviation (MAD): $$\text{MAD}(r) = \text{median}(|r_i - \text{median}(r)|)$$ Under a normal distribution $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$, the expected value of $\text{median}(|r_i - \text{median}(r)|)$ is $\Phi^{-1}(0.75) \cdot \sigma \approx 0.6745 \cdot \sigma$. To make the MAD an asymptotically unbiased estimator of $\sigma$ under Gaussian errors, it is scaled by the consistency factor: $$\hat{\sigma} = \frac{\text{MAD}(r)}{\Phi^{-1}(0.75)} \approx 1.4826 \cdot \text{median}(|r_i - \text{median}(r)|)$$ In R, `mad(res)` automatically includes this scaling factor by default. ### Weight Calculation: Huber's $\psi$-Function A standard choice for M-estimation is Huber's $\psi$-function, defined for a tuning constant $k$ (typically $k = 1.345$, yielding $95\%$ efficiency on normal data) as: $$\psi(z) = \begin{cases} z & \text{if } |z| \le k \\ k \cdot \text{sign}(z) & \text{if } |z| > k \end{cases}$$ The corresponding weight function $w(z) = \psi(z) / z$ evaluates to: $$w(z) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } |z| \le k \\ \frac{k}{|z|} & \text{if } |z| > k \end{cases}$$ Observations with residuals within $[-k, k]$ standard deviations receive full weight ($w_i = 1$), behaving like ordinary least squares. Points beyond $k$ receive weights inversely proportional to their residual distance, bounding their influence on the estimating equations. ## R Implementation The following implementation initializes the model with standard OLS and runs 10 iterations of the IRLS loop. In practice, the loop runs until the change in coefficients between iterations falls below a tolerance threshold. ```r # Initialize with standard OLS lmMod <- ols for (k in 1:10) { # 1. Extract residuals from the current fit res <- lmMod$res # 2. Compute the robust scale estimator (MAD) # mad(res) computes median(abs(res - median(res))) * 1.4826 stdev <- mad(res) # 3. Standardize residuals z <- res / stdev # 4. Calculate robust weights using Huber's psi w <- psi.huber(z) # 5. Fit a weighted linear model with updated weights lmMod <- lm(y ~ x, weights = w) # 6. Monitor convergence against references plot(x, y) abline(ols, lwd = 2) # Initial OLS (black) abline(mEst, col = "red", lwd = 2) # Library M-estimator reference (red) abline(lmMod, col = "blue", lwd = 2) # Current IRLS iteration (blue) legend("topleft", legend = c("OLS", "M-estimation", "Our Impl"), lwd = 2, col = c("black", "red", "blue")) } ``` Within a few iterations, the line obtained from this implementation (`Our Impl`, blue) converges to the reference robust fit (`mEst`, red), rotating away from leverage outliers and fitting the dominant trend of the data. ## Sources - Lecture script and slide notes: `=== NOTES: repeat this many times ===` (covering the IRLS loop, scale calculation via MAD consistency factor 1.4826, `psi.huber` weights, and sequential `lm(weights=w)` fits).
